content.text: The latest commit itself is data-only; it exposed a real crossover on the new 8-vCPU runner. The scheduled batch deduplicates thousands of compilations (4,345 hits) but still loses by ~34s because six fresh targets repeatedly hash and materialize the same outputs while eight compiler processes are already saturating the box. I’m narrowing whether the dominant fix belongs in cache-hit materialization or in permit allocation before changing code.

content.text: The fix is now implemented: once a completed compiler flight has published a usable prediction, waiting builds release that lock before restoring into their separate targets. This removes a hidden per-crate restore convoy while preserving serialization for actual compilation and failed/no-result flights. Unit tests pass; I’m setting up an A/B contention run against `main` before I publish the PR.

content.text: The A/B run disproved that first fix: releasing restore waiters increased the local batch from 117.8s to 132.6s and caused extra unscheduled probe bursts, so I’m discarding it. That result sharpens the diagnosis: the page’s large jump is primarily the runner change (32 vCPU → 8 vCPU), and the remaining within-run loss is the cost of six independent target trees on a small machine—not a newly slower scheduler critical section.

content.text:
The apparent regression isn’t caused by the latest code. The most recent commit, [#347](https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/pull/347), only refreshed benchmark JSON.

The numbers became incomparable because the benchmark moved from a 32-vCPU Namespace runner to a self-hosted container restricted to 8 CPUs:

| Runner | Sequential | Scheduled |
|---|---:|---:|
| Previous, 32 vCPU | 55.4s | 39.8s |
| Current, 8 vCPU | 269.0s | 302.8s |

On eight CPUs, sequential execution also reuses one Cargo target, whereas the parallel scenario maintains six separate targets. Although mbx deduplicated 4,345 compilations, it still restored 6,163 files totaling 3.66 GB. That overhead outweighs parallelism on this smaller machine. The [benchmark run](https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/actions/runs/33890632748) confirms the scheduler still bounds compilers correctly; unscheduled execution took 724.5s.

I tested two product changes:

- Parallelizing completed-flight restores: regressed locally from 117.8s to 132.6s and exceeded the benchmark’s compiler bound.
- Charging restores against scheduler permits: 117.845s → 117.789s, effectively noise.

I discarded both and left the repository clean. I did not create a PR because neither change demonstrated a real performance improvement. The honest fix is benchmarking future contention results on the original 32-vCPU class—or establishing a new 8-vCPU baseline—rather than changing production scheduling to chase a hardware-induced comparison.
